nameStory: The white fringetree gets its delightful name from its spectacular spring flowers that look exactly like delicate white fringe or tassels hanging from the branches. Each flower has four long, narrow petals that flutter in the breeze like silky ribbons, creating one of nature's most elegant displays.
description: White fringetree is a small native tree or large shrub that puts on one of the most stunning flower shows in late spring. It typically grows 12-25 feet tall with a rounded, open crown and smooth gray bark. The tree is covered in clusters of fragrant, drooping white flowers that look like cotton fringe, followed by dark blue berry-like fruits that wildlife love.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Drooping clusters of pure white flowers with four extremely narrow, strap-like petals that hang like delicate fringe or tassels. The flowers are sweetly fragrant and appear in late May to early June before the leaves are fully developed.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple, oval leaves arranged opposite each other on the branches, measuring 3-8 inches long. They feel smooth and leathery with a glossy dark green surface that turns bright yellow in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark blue to purple berry-like fruits (technically drupes) about half an inch long that hang in loose clusters in late summer. They have a waxy coating and contain a large seed inside.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, light gray bark that remains relatively smooth even on older trunks, sometimes developing shallow furrows. The bark has a clean, almost polished appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small tree or large multi-stemmed shrub with an open, airy crown and somewhat irregular branching pattern. Often wider than it is tall when grown in the open.

habitat: In New England, white fringetree is rare and found mainly in southern areas, particularly in moist, well-drained soils along woodland edges, stream banks, and in partially shaded locations. It prefers acidic soils and is often found growing with other understory trees like dogwood and redbud in mixed hardwood forests.

seasonality.spring: The spectacular white fringe-like flowers appear in late May to early June, creating drooping clusters that are unmistakable and highly fragrant. New leaves emerge as glossy, bright green ovals.
seasonality.summer: Foliage is full and lush with dark green, leathery leaves. Small green fruits begin developing after the flowers fade, gradually enlarging through the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, and the dark blue fruits ripen and become very attractive to birds. The fruit clusters hang prominently on bare branches after leaf drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the tree's open, irregular structure with smooth gray bark. Old fruit clusters may persist, and the opposite branching pattern becomes clearly visible.

funFact: White fringetree is sometimes called 'grancy graybeard' in the South because the masses of drooping white flowers supposedly resemble an old man's flowing white beard - and some trees are either all male or all female, so only the female trees produce the beautiful blue fruits!
confusionNotes: The unique fringe-like flowers make this tree nearly impossible to confuse with anything else when in bloom. Out of flower, the opposite leaves and smooth bark might remind you of dogwood, but dogwood has distinctly veined leaves while fringetree's are smooth and leathery.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the olive family, white fringetree is completely unrelated to olives you eat, though both share the characteristic opposite leaves. This native tree is becoming increasingly popular in landscaping but remains quite rare in the wild in New England, making any sighting special.
compareHints: White fringetree is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique in the region. Within the olive family, it's most similar to ash trees, but ash trees have compound leaves while fringetree has simple leaves, and no ash tree produces anything remotely like the spectacular fringe flowers.
